newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bills of exchange trade seen slow to year-end.
newsitem.headline: Thai bills of exchange trade seen slow to year-end.

text.p: Trading in bills of exchange in Thailand will remain sluggish for the rest of the year because of continuing political and economic uncertainties in the domestic market, finance industry sources said.

"Activity in the bills of exchange market has declined sharply over the past few weeks. I don't think it will pick up over the next few months," a bills of exchange trader at the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand told Reuters.
She said foreign interest in bills of exchange had slowed due to a flight of foreign capital from Thailand and tight liquidity sparked by the current political and economic flux.
Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa, whose six-party coalition government had been blamed for many of the economic woes facing the country, called fresh elections last Friday.
With an election set for November 17, only a caretaker government will be in place and market players are unsure of what type of government might emerge from the upcoming polls, analysts said.
"The political and economic picture will be still unclear in the near term. Foreigners will not come back until all is resolved," said one senior treasurer at a local brokerage.

Bills of exchange are short-term debt instruments. They are orders given in exchange for funds raised and promise to pay a specified amount of money to holders either at a set future date or on demand when presented for payment.
The bills have gained a strong following in Thailand, especially among foreign investors since late last year, because they carry attractive interest rates and are highly marketable, analysts said.
Foreign investors, however, have cut their exposure to the bills in recent times because of rumours the baht may be devalued in order to boost Thailand's sagging exports.

Doubts about the financial health of some local finance companies which surfaced late July also triggered withdrawals, analysts said. Finance firms are the biggest issuers of billions of dollars worth of bills of exchange now in circulation in the country.
The withdrawals took place despite denials by the Bank of Thailand and the Stock Exchange of Thailand.
Moves by the central bank to curb short-term foreign fund inflows would also have a major impact on the bills of exchange business, analysts said.
"The Bank of Thailand does not want a large amount of money raised via bill of exchanges because they are regarded as short-term funds," said another treasurer at a major finance company.
But most analysts believed the bills still appeared to be attractive short-term instruments for foreign investors because of their high yields.
"The spread of 5-6 percent between Thai and foreign short-term interest rates will still draw foreign investor interest in them," the treasurer said.
